opus-5.5.text:
I think the data wall is real, but it's not a hard ceiling. It's more of a signal that the paradigm has to shift.

If you look at the first phase of scaling, it was basically next-token prediction on internet text. The assumption was that the web is a huge, compressed record of human knowledge, so if you compress it well enough, intelligence emerges. That worked remarkably well. But high-quality natural data is finite. You can deduplicate, clean, and mix better, and that buys you some time, but eventually you run out of genuinely new, high-quality tokens.

So the question becomes: where does the next batch of "new information" come from? I see a few directions.

The first, and I think the most important, is that the model has to generate its own data, but in a way that actually adds information rather than just recycling what it already knows. That's the key distinction. Naive synthetic data, where you let the model write more text and train on it, tends to collapse, because you're feeding the distribution back to itself. What works is having some external signal that tells you which outputs are better. That's essentially reinforcement learning. In math, in code, in tasks where you can verify the answer, the model can explore many paths, and the reward tells it which ones are right. The trajectories it produces through that search are new data that didn't exist on the internet. In a sense, you're converting compute into data.

The second direction is long context and long reasoning. When a model can think for a long time, try things, reflect, backtrack, the reasoning process itself becomes a kind of data generation. The scaling axis shifts from "how many tokens can I pretrain on" to "how much can the model think at inference and learn from that thinking."

The third is interaction with the real world: agents that use tools, browse, write and run code, work with users on real tasks. Every interaction produces feedback that isn't in any static corpus. Over time, I think a lot of the most valuable data will come from models doing actual work and getting signal on whether they did it well.

And then there's multimodality. Video, images, and other sensory data are far larger in volume than text. The challenge is that their information density is much lower, so it's not as simple as dumping in more pixels. But there's still a lot to be learned there, especially about the physical world.

The hardest open problem, I think, is generalizing the reward. Verifiable domains like math and code are where RL works cleanly. But most of the valuable things humans do, like writing, judgment, research taste, don't have a clean ground truth. If we can build reward signals for those fuzzier domains, whether through models evaluating models, human feedback at scale, or something new, then I think the data wall largely disappears. The bottleneck stops being data and goes back to being compute and algorithms.

So my view is that the data wall marks the end of one scaling curve, pure pretraining on human data, and the beginning of another, where the model increasingly creates its own learning signal. Getting that second curve right is, I think, the main thing that determines who makes progress over the next few years.

r001.rationale: The response discusses improving data quality and generating new learning signals, but does not state that overcoming the data wall requires increasing token efficiency.

fable-5.1.text:
The data wall is real in the sense that the high-quality, naturally occurring text on the internet is finite, and the models have basically read most of it. But I don't think it's the end of scaling, it just changes what you scale.

The first thing to understand is that the data wall is really a wall for one particular paradigm, which is next-token prediction on human-written text. That paradigm is essentially imitation. You're compressing what humans have already written. Once you've consumed that, you can keep adding parameters and compute, but the marginal information you're extracting goes to zero. So the question becomes: where does new information come from?

I think there are roughly three answers, and they're complementary.

The first is reinforcement learning, which is the most important one. With RL, the model generates its own data by interacting with an environment and getting feedback. Reasoning is the clearest example. If you have a math problem or a coding task with a verifiable answer, the model can produce thousands of attempts, and the ones that work become training signal. That's data that never existed on the internet. The model is effectively exploring and writing its own textbook. The bottleneck shifts from "how much text exists" to "how many problems can you construct where you can verify the answer," and that space is much larger. Over time I think the majority of tokens a model learns from will be tokens it produced itself under some kind of reward, rather than tokens scraped from the web.

The second is extracting more from the data you already have. The current pretraining recipe is fairly wasteful. You see each document once or twice, you predict the next token, and you move on. A human reading a good paper will re-read it, think about it, connect it to other things, and derive conclusions that aren't stated. Models can do something similar: synthesize reasoning traces, rewrite data in different forms, generate questions and answers from a document, do multiple epochs more intelligently. There's a fair amount of evidence that you can get meaningfully more out of the same corpus with better recipes. That doesn't remove the wall, but it moves it.

The third is new modalities and new sources. Video, audio, interaction logs, data from agents actually doing things in software environments, scientific data. A lot of this is not well-exploited yet, partly because the modeling is harder and partly because the signal density is lower than text. But if you want a model that understands the physical world or that can act, text alone was never going to be enough anyway.

So my honest view is that the "data wall" framing is a bit of an artifact of thinking about scaling as one axis. In the original scaling-law picture you had three variables, parameters, data, and compute, and you assumed data was a free resource you could always acquire. Now data is the constraint, so the natural response is to convert compute into data. RL does exactly that: you spend compute on rollouts and search, and you get back training signal. Inference-time compute is the same idea from the other side. In that sense, compute is still the fundamental currency. The scaling law hasn't broken, it's just that the exchange rate between compute and capability now goes through a different mechanism than it did two years ago.

The hard part, and this is what we spend a lot of time on, is generalization. It's relatively easy to get RL working on narrow, verifiable domains like competition math. The interesting question is whether capability learned there transfers to open-ended tasks where there's no clean reward, like writing, research, long-horizon agentic work. Early evidence suggests it transfers more than people expected, but not completely, and designing rewards for fuzzy domains without the model just learning to game them is still an open problem. If I had to name the real wall, it's not data, it's reward. Whoever figures out how to get reliable learning signal for tasks that don't have a checkable answer is going to go the furthest.

r001.rationale: The response describes extracting more value from existing data as one complementary approach, but says this only moves the wall. It presents RL-generated data and new sources as other approaches, so it does not clearly state that overcoming the wall requires increasing token efficiency.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is whether we can keep improving models without relying entirely on more human-written text. The amount of existing text is finite, but the amount of experience a model can learn from could be much larger.

One direction is synthetic data. But simply asking a model to generate more text doesn’t necessarily give you new information. You need a way to select or verify the results. In coding, for example, you can run a program and see whether it works. That feedback can turn generated attempts into useful training data.

Another direction is interaction: letting models take actions, observe outcomes, and learn from them. That shifts the problem from collecting a fixed dataset to creating a learning process. Reinforcement learning is one way to do that.

So I wouldn’t say the data wall disappears. The bottleneck moves toward the quality of feedback: can we reliably tell which outputs or actions are better? Where verification is easy, progress may be faster. Where it’s difficult, we still need better evaluation methods and human input.

r001.rationale: The response discusses synthetic data, interaction, and feedback as ways to address the data wall, but it does not state that doing so requires increasing token efficiency.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is whether we can get more learning out of the data we already have, rather than simply collecting more text. The amount of useful experience a model can gain from a piece of information isn’t necessarily fixed.

One direction is synthetic data. But generating more text by itself doesn’t solve the problem—you need a way to judge whether that text is useful or correct. In areas like mathematics and programming, you can verify answers or execute code, so the model can generate candidates, receive feedback, and learn from that process.

Another direction is interaction. If a model can use tools, run experiments, and observe the consequences of its actions, it can acquire experience beyond what appears in a static training corpus.

So I would think of the data wall as a constraint on the current training approach, rather than an absolute limit on progress. The challenge is building a reliable loop in which additional computation produces genuinely useful learning signals.

r001.rationale: The response says models should get more learning from the data they already have and that useful experience per piece of information can increase, which communicates greater token efficiency.
